transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been going on that made you decide to come see me?

Hi, nice to meet you. Well, I guess the main thing that pushed me to come in is what's happening at work. I process insurance claims, and I just... I keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, I know I’m supposed to stay put and actually finish my claim reviews, but I just keep leaving my desk. It's really starting to become a problem for me.
When you get the urge to leave your desk, does it feel like something you can't control or resist, or does it feel more like you're choosing to leave even though you know you shouldn't?

I guess it's more like I'm choosing to leave, even though I know I shouldn't. Like I mentioned, I know I’m supposed to stay put and actually finish my claim reviews. It's not like a physical force is pulling me out of my chair or anything, but... I just keep getting up from my workstation anyway. It's just really hard for me to stay seated and get the work done.
When you're sitting at your desk trying to work, are you able to focus on the insurance claims themselves, or do you find your mind wandering and having trouble concentrating on the task?

Yeah, my mind definitely wanders. It's like... if people near me start talking about another claim, or even if I just suddenly remember some random errand I need to run, my attention just slides right off what I'm looking at. I usually end up having to reread the same section of a file a few times before it actually registers.
How long have you been experiencing this difficulty concentrating and staying focused? Has this always been something you've struggled with, or is this something newer that started more recently?

Well, the problems at work specifically... they've been going on for about 15 months now. That's when my department went through a big reorganization. Before that, I don't know, maybe I struggled a little, but it really became an issue after that reshuffle.
Before that reorganization 15 months ago, when you were in your old department, did you have similar trouble staying focused and sitting still, or was that really not an issue for you back then?

Well, looking back... it wasn't exactly brand new for me. I mean, I guess it wasn't as big of a problem at work before the reorganization, but I've always kind of struggled with this stuff. Like, in elementary school, my teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright, but... I was always losing my worksheets or missing instructions. They were constantly having to remind me to just finish my classwork. So I guess the focus thing has been around for a long time.

When you were in elementary school and your teachers were reminding you to finish your classwork, were you also the kind of kid who had trouble sitting still? Like, did you fidget a lot or feel restless when you had to stay in your seat?

Um, I don't remember exactly how much I moved around as a kid, but I definitely do that kind of thing now. Like, if I'm in a training or one of our longer team meetings at work, I'm usually bouncing my leg or clicking my pen. I just end up shifting around in my chair a lot, even when I'm really trying to look focused.
When you were in elementary school, did your teachers or parents ever mention that you were hyperactive, restless, or that you had trouble sitting still in class or at home?

I really don't recall anyone ever saying I was hyperactive back then. It was mostly just the losing things and not finishing my work that they talked about. I don't think sitting still was a major issue for me as a kid, or at least no one ever brought it up to me or my parents that I know of.

You mentioned you bounce your leg, click your pen, and shift around in your chair during meetings at work now. When did that start happening—was that also something that picked up around the time of the reorganization 15 months ago, or have you been doing those kinds of fidgety movements for most of your life?

I'm really not sure, to be honest. I can't pinpoint exactly when it started. I guess it's possible it picked up around the time of the reorganization, or maybe I've been doing it for a while and just didn't really notice until lately. I just don't have a clear memory of when that specific stuff began.

Looking back at your childhood and teenage years, do you remember being someone who was generally restless or fidgety in situations where you had to sit still—like during car rides, family dinners, or watching TV—even if teachers didn't specifically call it out as a problem?

No, I really don't think so. I mean, looking back at being a kid or a teenager, I don't remember feeling restless or having a hard time sitting still during things like car rides or dinners. It just wasn't really something I struggled with back then.

When you're in situations outside of work now—like at home watching TV, during family gatherings, or doing hobbies you enjoy—do you notice yourself fidgeting, bouncing your leg, or shifting around the same way you do at work?

Um, no, not really. I haven't noticed it happening at home. If I'm just watching TV or doing something I actually enjoy, I don't think I'm bouncing my leg or shifting around like I do at the office. It seems to mostly just be a work thing.

You mentioned the fidgeting mostly happens at work. When you're in other situations that are stressful or demanding—like during a difficult conversation, paying bills at home, or doing something that requires concentration outside of work—do you notice yourself fidgeting or feeling restless then, or is it really just limited to your work environment?

I think it really is just limited to work. Like I said before, it's mostly in trainings or those longer team meetings. That's when I'm usually bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or just shifting around in my chair a lot, even when I'm really trying to look like I'm focused on what's going on. I don't really notice myself doing that stuff when I'm paying bills or doing other things at home.

When you're doing something at home that requires you to really concentrate and stay focused—like reading something important, doing taxes, or working on a hobby project that demands attention—do you find your mind wandering or do you feel the urge to get up and move around, or does your concentration stay pretty steady in those situations?

Honestly, my concentration isn't great at home either, but I wouldn't say I feel the urge to get up and move around. Like if I'm doing taxes or trying to read something important, my mind definitely wanders off. I'll just zone out or start thinking about something else entirely. But I don't really get that restless, fidgety feeling like I need to get up and pace or anything. I just lose focus.

In elementary school, did you ever get sent to the principal's office, get detention, or have any formal behavioral or academic interventions because of not paying attention or not finishing your work?

No, I never got sent to the principal's office or had detention or anything major like that. But, um, looking back, the attention stuff wasn't exactly brand new. I remember my elementary school teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright, but I was always losing my worksheets or missing instructions. They were always having to give me reminders to actually finish my classwork. So, it was there, just not in a way that got me in trouble.

Besides school, when you were a kid, did your parents ever notice or mention that you had trouble paying attention or following instructions at home—like during homework, chores, or family activities?

My parents didn't really say anything about it, honestly. I don't remember them ever bringing up that I had trouble paying attention at home. Homework just got done eventually, and chores were just normal chores. They never made a big deal out of me not following instructions or anything like that.

When you were in elementary school and your teachers were writing on your report cards about you losing worksheets and missing instructions, was that happening across multiple grades, or was it more of a thing that happened in just one or two grades before it got better?

Yeah, it was definitely across multiple grades. It wasn't just a one-time thing. Like I said, looking back, this wasn't exactly brand new for me. Pretty much throughout elementary school, my teachers used to write the same kind of stuff—that I was a bright kid, but I was always losing my worksheets, missing the instructions they just gave, and constantly needing reminders to actually finish my classwork. It was kind of a running theme, not just one or two years.

When you were in elementary school and having trouble with losing worksheets and missing instructions at school, do you remember having similar kinds of problems outside of school—like forgetting things at home, having trouble following your parents' instructions, or losing your belongings in general?

No, not really. Like I said before, my parents never really brought up anything about me having trouble paying attention or following instructions at home. I don't remember losing my stuff outside of school or having issues with chores or anything. It really just seemed to be a problem when I was in the classroom.

When you were in elementary school and your teachers were writing those report cards about you losing worksheets and missing instructions, how much of a problem was it? Like, were you falling behind in your grades, or were you still doing okay academically despite needing those reminders?

I don't really remember it being a huge issue with my actual grades. I mean, from what I recall, I was still doing okay academically. It was... I think it was mostly just the teachers pointing out that I needed those extra reminders to actually finish the work, but I wasn't really falling behind or failing classes or anything like that.

When you think back to your elementary school years, besides the trouble with losing worksheets and missing instructions at school, did you have any difficulty focusing or paying attention during activities you actually enjoyed—like playing games, sports, hobbies, or things you were interested in?

No, I don't think I had any issues there. If it was something I actually liked doing, you know, like playing video games or just hanging out, I could focus on it just fine. I don't remember ever having trouble paying attention to the fun stuff. It was really just the schoolwork that I struggled with.

When you were in elementary school, do you remember being someone who would interrupt people a lot, or act without thinking things through first—like blurting things out in class or doing things impulsively without considering the consequences?

No, I don't think so. I wasn't really the type to blurt things out or interrupt people. I was actually pretty quiet in class, for the most part. I don't remember ever getting in trouble for acting out or doing things without thinking.
